intuition.text: The net reaction shown by the authors consumes Al and NH4Cl in a 1:1 ratio, whereas their best experimental charge ratio is NH4Cl:Al = 3:1. Lower-ratio diffraction patterns retain unreacted Al. The authors associate at least 3:1 with more complete reaction; this is an empirical feed condition, not a revised stoichiometric equation.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Equation 1; Figure 4 and feed-ratio discussion

intuition.title: Proposed chloride-mediated nitridation
intuition.text: The authors propose NH4Cl decomposition followed by chloridization of Al and reaction of volatile aluminum chlorides with NH3. The cited 339 °C decomposition value, subchloride equilibrium and gas–gas growth picture are contextual hypotheses. No transient aluminum-chloride species, gas composition or mechanism is directly measured. All seven source equations remain accessible in the source context.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Equations 1–7 and mechanism discussion

intuition.title: Pressure, crystallization and particle growth
intuition.text: The paper proposes that increasing NH4Cl raises autoclave pressure and benefits crystallization, but reports no measured pressure. At about 500 °C the AlN has very poor crystallinity; the selected method uses 580 °C. Increasing temperature is described as growing particles and improving crystallinity, without a numerical size-versus-temperature series.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Feed-ratio and processing-temperature discussions

intuition.title: Different size measurements answer different questions
intuition.text: The 6 nm Scherrer estimate describes diffraction coherence; the rounded 6 nm TEM mean and the 5.85 nm histogram-derived mean describe particle projections. The histogram spans 3–11 nm and reports a standard deviation of 0.57 without an explicit unit. These observations are kept distinct instead of being averaged into one invented measurement.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figures 1–3 and size discussion

intuition.title: Commercial precursor oxidation and impurity
intuition.text: Small oxide reflections are attributed as a possibility to surface oxidation of the commercial Al powder. The source distinguishes oxide impurity from the residual Al associated with incomplete reaction at lower NH4Cl feeds. Neither impurity fraction nor precursor oxide coverage is quantified.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Figures 1 and 4 impurity assignments

intuition.title: Application motivation and future scope
intuition.text: AlN thermal, electrical and mechanical properties motivate the synthesis through cited literature; no new functional-property or device tests are reported here. Suggested extensions to Si3N4, BN and GaN are outlook statements, not prepared products or recipes.

intuition.title: Proposed phase transfer, reduction and recovery
intuition.text: The authors describe a liquid ethanol/linoleic-acid phase, solid sodium linoleate and a water/ethanol phase containing Ag ions. They propose Ag-ion exchange into silver linoleate, reduction by ethanol at interfaces, outward-facing alkyl chains and gravity-assisted phase separation. These are the paper’s mechanism interpretation; silver linoleate, ligand coverage and phase compositions were not directly measured.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied PDF p. 2, hydrothermal preparation and mechanism

intuition.title: Particle cores and assembled monolayers are distinct
intuition.text: The TEM specimen shows round, smooth Ag particles, a reported diameter of 5.0 ± 0.3 nm and ordered arrays on a carbon-film/Cu support. The ± statistic is unspecified. The authors interpret the smooth packing as diffusion outpacing arrival during grid drying; it does not establish a measured diffusion coefficient or a separate synthesis.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied PDF pp. 2–3, TEM method, Figure 1 and packing discussion

intuition.title: Surface identity remains unresolved
intuition.text: The preparation and Figure 2 discussion describe linoleic-acid passivation, while Figure 1 and the interlinking discussion refer to sodium linoleate tails. Both descriptions are kept as source-proposed context; neither is a measured bound-ligand structure or a resolved identity assignment.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied PDF pp. 2–3, Figure 1 caption, passivation and Figure 2 discussion

intuition.title: Spacing and weak plasmon absorption
intuition.text: The source reports a center-separation/particle-diameter ratio D/2r of approximately 1.75. It associates weak plasmon absorption with small particle cores and ordered separation. No absolute interparticle gap, shell thickness, quantitative coupling constant or absorption-peak wavelength is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied PDF pp. 3–4, Figure 3 and D/2r discussion

intuition.title: PL explanation is a hypothesis
intuition.text: The measured 390 nm PL band is obtained with 250 nm excitation on quartz. The authors propose radiative sp-electron/d-hole recombination enhanced by a combination of surface plasmon and an electrostatic mechanism analogous to SERS. This source does not supply its own Raman measurement, absolute PL quantum yield or time-resolved mechanism test.
intuition.source_locator: Supplied PDF pp. 3–4, optical methods and mechanism

intuition.title: Cited variations do not become new recipes
intuition.text: Temperature control of core size, alternative fatty-acid/sodium-stearate combinations and electronic transitions appear as cited discussion, including an unpublished reference. No separate source-defined charge, temperature series or measured conductivity outcome is supplied here.

intuition.title: Surface area and reaction completion
intuition.text: The authors link the greater reactivity of nano-Al to its high surface area. Nano-Al converts fully under their 1000–1100 °C conditions, while coarse commercial feedstocks retain local excess Al even when powder XRD shows only AlN reflections. The smaller feedstock does not imply that its original size survives: partially reacted Al/AlN droplets are 5–15 µm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nitridation, footnote 11 and partial-reaction discussion

intuition.title: AlCl3 as a proposed vapor-transport reagent
intuition.text: AlCl3 addition favors whisker growth and changes partially reacted droplet shapes. The proposed Figure 2 transport cycle involves volatile AlCl and AlCl3, with AlN deposition from vapor. These transient species and reaction pathways are proposed from morphology and cited equilibria, not directly measured intermediates.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 2 and vapor-transport discussion

intuition.title: Heating rate changes the reaction history
intuition.text: Rapid heating is proposed to reduce the time available for Al particles to coalesce and for AlCl3 to sublime away before nitridation begins. The source places reaction onset around 1073 K, about 140 K above Al melting. This mechanistic onset is not a new specimen-specific synthesis schedule.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Heating-rate explanation

intuition.title: Why the authors favor vapor–solid growth
intuition.text: No flux droplets were seen at whisker tips, unspecified potential flux materials did not promote whiskers, and diverse branching directions were observed. These observations favor the authors’ vapor–solid interpretation over vapor–liquid–solid growth; they do not identify every unseen intermediate or provide a tested list of flux reagents.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker-growth mechanism discussion

intuition.title: Measured geometry, a model input and size ranges
intuition.text: The 40–180 nm Scherrer range, 10–200 nm TEM crystallites and 0.5–5 µm aggregates describe different bases in the nano-Al series. Footnote 6 separately labels a 28 nm analytical input. A 44 nm input appears in a Kelvin-equation argument predicting only a 2–3% equilibrium vapor-pressure increase; it is not a new synthetic specimen. The authors instead propose enhanced nonequilibrium steady-state vapor pressure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nano-Al characterization, footnote 6 and Kelvin discussion

intuition.title: Whiskers versus polycrystalline fibers
intuition.text: SAD establishes single crystallinity for the examined whiskers; study-wide whisker diameters are generally 20–100 nm with aspect ratios 20 to greater than 100. SEM alone cannot establish whether the stubble on partially nitrided Al droplets is single-crystal whiskers. TEM fragments show that some similar material is polycrystalline fibers. These observations remain separate rather than relabeling all fibers as whiskers.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker dimensions, partial-reaction discussion and footnote 14

intuition.title: Scope of practical implications
intuition.text: The paper demonstrates morphological control by varying feed size, chloride addition and ramp rate. It does not measure device, thermal, optical or mechanical performance of the resulting particles. The precursor preparation also has a source-reported explosion warning; the referenced six-page SI with detailed precautions and synthetic procedures remains unreviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction, conclusion, footnote 5 and supporting-information notice

intuition.title: Surface area and reaction completion
intuition.text: The authors link the greater reactivity of nano-Al to its high surface area. Nano-Al converts fully under their 1000–1100 °C conditions, while coarse commercial feedstocks retain local excess Al even when powder XRD shows only AlN reflections. The smaller feedstock does not imply that its original size survives: partially reacted Al/AlN droplets are 5–15 µm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nitridation, footnote 11 and partial-reaction discussion

intuition.title: AlCl3 as a proposed vapor-transport reagent
intuition.text: AlCl3 addition favors whisker growth and changes partially reacted droplet shapes. The proposed Figure 2 transport cycle involves volatile AlCl and AlCl3, with AlN deposition from vapor. These transient species and reaction pathways are proposed from morphology and cited equilibria, not directly measured intermediates.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 2 and vapor-transport discussion

intuition.title: Heating rate changes the reaction history
intuition.text: Rapid heating is proposed to reduce the time available for Al particles to coalesce and for AlCl3 to sublime away before nitridation begins. The source places reaction onset around 1073 K, about 140 K above Al melting. This mechanistic onset is not a new specimen-specific synthesis schedule.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Heating-rate explanation

intuition.title: Why the authors favor vapor–solid growth
intuition.text: No flux droplets were seen at whisker tips, unspecified potential flux materials did not promote whiskers, and diverse branching directions were observed. These observations favor the authors’ vapor–solid interpretation over vapor–liquid–solid growth; they do not identify every unseen intermediate or provide a tested list of flux reagents.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker-growth mechanism discussion

intuition.title: Measured geometry, a model input and size ranges
intuition.text: The 40–180 nm Scherrer range, 10–200 nm TEM crystallites and 0.5–5 µm aggregates describe different bases in the nano-Al series. Footnote 6 separately labels a 28 nm analytical input. A 44 nm input appears in a Kelvin-equation argument predicting only a 2–3% equilibrium vapor-pressure increase; it is not a new synthetic specimen. The authors instead propose enhanced nonequilibrium steady-state vapor pressure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nano-Al characterization, footnote 6 and Kelvin discussion

intuition.title: Whiskers versus polycrystalline fibers
intuition.text: SAD establishes single crystallinity for the examined whiskers; study-wide whisker diameters are generally 20–100 nm with aspect ratios 20 to greater than 100. SEM alone cannot establish whether the stubble on partially nitrided Al droplets is single-crystal whiskers. TEM fragments show that some similar material is polycrystalline fibers. These observations remain separate rather than relabeling all fibers as whiskers.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker dimensions, partial-reaction discussion and footnote 14

intuition.title: Scope of practical implications
intuition.text: The paper demonstrates morphological control by varying feed size, chloride addition and ramp rate. It does not measure device, thermal, optical or mechanical performance of the resulting particles. The precursor preparation also has a source-reported explosion warning; the referenced six-page SI with detailed precautions and synthetic procedures remains unreviewed.

intuition.title: Surface area and reaction completion
intuition.text: The authors link the greater reactivity of nano-Al to its high surface area. Nano-Al converts fully under their 1000–1100 °C conditions, while coarse commercial feedstocks retain local excess Al even when powder XRD shows only AlN reflections. The smaller feedstock does not imply that its original size survives: partially reacted Al/AlN droplets are 5–15 µm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nitridation, footnote 11 and partial-reaction discussion

intuition.title: AlCl3 as a proposed vapor-transport reagent
intuition.text: AlCl3 addition favors whisker growth and changes partially reacted droplet shapes. The proposed Figure 2 transport cycle involves volatile AlCl and AlCl3, with AlN deposition from vapor. These transient species and reaction pathways are proposed from morphology and cited equilibria, not directly measured intermediates.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 2 and vapor-transport discussion

intuition.title: Heating rate changes the reaction history
intuition.text: Rapid heating is proposed to reduce the time available for Al particles to coalesce and for AlCl3 to sublime away before nitridation begins. The source places reaction onset around 1073 K, about 140 K above Al melting. This mechanistic onset is not a new specimen-specific synthesis schedule.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Heating-rate explanation

intuition.title: Why the authors favor vapor–solid growth
intuition.text: No flux droplets were seen at whisker tips, unspecified potential flux materials did not promote whiskers, and diverse branching directions were observed. These observations favor the authors’ vapor–solid interpretation over vapor–liquid–solid growth; they do not identify every unseen intermediate or provide a tested list of flux reagents.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker-growth mechanism discussion

intuition.title: Measured geometry, a model input and size ranges
intuition.text: The 40–180 nm Scherrer range, 10–200 nm TEM crystallites and 0.5–5 µm aggregates describe different bases in the nano-Al series. Footnote 6 separately labels a 28 nm analytical input. A 44 nm input appears in a Kelvin-equation argument predicting only a 2–3% equilibrium vapor-pressure increase; it is not a new synthetic specimen. The authors instead propose enhanced nonequilibrium steady-state vapor pressure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nano-Al characterization, footnote 6 and Kelvin discussion

intuition.title: Whiskers versus polycrystalline fibers
intuition.text: SAD establishes single crystallinity for the examined whiskers; study-wide whisker diameters are generally 20–100 nm with aspect ratios 20 to greater than 100. SEM alone cannot establish whether the stubble on partially nitrided Al droplets is single-crystal whiskers. TEM fragments show that some similar material is polycrystalline fibers. These observations remain separate rather than relabeling all fibers as whiskers.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker dimensions, partial-reaction discussion and footnote 14

intuition.title: Scope of practical implications
intuition.text: The paper demonstrates morphological control by varying feed size, chloride addition and ramp rate. It does not measure device, thermal, optical or mechanical performance of the resulting particles. The precursor preparation also has a source-reported explosion warning; the referenced six-page SI with detailed precautions and synthetic procedures remains unreviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction, conclusion, footnote 5 and supporting-information notice

intuition.title: Study-wide AlN diffraction-coherence range
intuition.text: The source reports 25–50 nm mean XRD coherence lengths for nano-Al-derived AlN formed at 1000–1100 °C. This precedes the separate morphology discussion and is not assigned as a Figure 1b or 20 °C/min specimen-specific fit. The full statement remains in source contexts, outside product-bound measurements.

intuition.title: Surface area and reaction completion
intuition.text: The authors link the greater reactivity of nano-Al to its high surface area. Nano-Al converts fully under their 1000–1100 °C conditions, while coarse commercial feedstocks retain local excess Al even when powder XRD shows only AlN reflections. The smaller feedstock does not imply that its original size survives: partially reacted Al/AlN droplets are 5–15 µm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nitridation, footnote 11 and partial-reaction discussion

intuition.title: AlCl3 as a proposed vapor-transport reagent
intuition.text: AlCl3 addition favors whisker growth and changes partially reacted droplet shapes. The proposed Figure 2 transport cycle involves volatile AlCl and AlCl3, with AlN deposition from vapor. These transient species and reaction pathways are proposed from morphology and cited equilibria, not directly measured intermediates.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 2 and vapor-transport discussion

intuition.title: Heating rate changes the reaction history
intuition.text: Rapid heating is proposed to reduce the time available for Al particles to coalesce and for AlCl3 to sublime away before nitridation begins. The source places reaction onset around 1073 K, about 140 K above Al melting. This mechanistic onset is not a new specimen-specific synthesis schedule.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Heating-rate explanation

intuition.title: Why the authors favor vapor–solid growth
intuition.text: No flux droplets were seen at whisker tips, unspecified potential flux materials did not promote whiskers, and diverse branching directions were observed. These observations favor the authors’ vapor–solid interpretation over vapor–liquid–solid growth; they do not identify every unseen intermediate or provide a tested list of flux reagents.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker-growth mechanism discussion

intuition.title: Measured geometry, a model input and size ranges
intuition.text: The 40–180 nm Scherrer range, 10–200 nm TEM crystallites and 0.5–5 µm aggregates describe different bases in the nano-Al series. Footnote 6 separately labels a 28 nm analytical input. A 44 nm input appears in a Kelvin-equation argument predicting only a 2–3% equilibrium vapor-pressure increase; it is not a new synthetic specimen. The authors instead propose enhanced nonequilibrium steady-state vapor pressure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nano-Al characterization, footnote 6 and Kelvin discussion

intuition.title: Whiskers versus polycrystalline fibers
intuition.text: SAD establishes single crystallinity for the examined whiskers; study-wide whisker diameters are generally 20–100 nm with aspect ratios 20 to greater than 100. SEM alone cannot establish whether the stubble on partially nitrided Al droplets is single-crystal whiskers. TEM fragments show that some similar material is polycrystalline fibers. These observations remain separate rather than relabeling all fibers as whiskers.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker dimensions, partial-reaction discussion and footnote 14

intuition.title: Scope of practical implications
intuition.text: The paper demonstrates morphological control by varying feed size, chloride addition and ramp rate. It does not measure device, thermal, optical or mechanical performance of the resulting particles. The precursor preparation also has a source-reported explosion warning; the referenced six-page SI with detailed precautions and synthetic procedures remains unreviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction, conclusion, footnote 5 and supporting-information notice

intuition.title: Surface area and reaction completion
intuition.text: The authors link the greater reactivity of nano-Al to its high surface area. Nano-Al converts fully under their 1000–1100 °C conditions, while coarse commercial feedstocks retain local excess Al even when powder XRD shows only AlN reflections. The smaller feedstock does not imply that its original size survives: partially reacted Al/AlN droplets are 5–15 µm.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nitridation, footnote 11 and partial-reaction discussion

intuition.title: AlCl3 as a proposed vapor-transport reagent
intuition.text: AlCl3 addition favors whisker growth and changes partially reacted droplet shapes. The proposed Figure 2 transport cycle involves volatile AlCl and AlCl3, with AlN deposition from vapor. These transient species and reaction pathways are proposed from morphology and cited equilibria, not directly measured intermediates.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 2 and vapor-transport discussion

intuition.title: Heating rate changes the reaction history
intuition.text: Rapid heating is proposed to reduce the time available for Al particles to coalesce and for AlCl3 to sublime away before nitridation begins. The source places reaction onset around 1073 K, about 140 K above Al melting. This mechanistic onset is not a new specimen-specific synthesis schedule.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Heating-rate explanation

intuition.title: Why the authors favor vapor–solid growth
intuition.text: No flux droplets were seen at whisker tips, unspecified potential flux materials did not promote whiskers, and diverse branching directions were observed. These observations favor the authors’ vapor–solid interpretation over vapor–liquid–solid growth; they do not identify every unseen intermediate or provide a tested list of flux reagents.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker-growth mechanism discussion

intuition.title: Measured geometry, a model input and size ranges
intuition.text: The 40–180 nm Scherrer range, 10–200 nm TEM crystallites and 0.5–5 µm aggregates describe different bases in the nano-Al series. Footnote 6 separately labels a 28 nm analytical input. A 44 nm input appears in a Kelvin-equation argument predicting only a 2–3% equilibrium vapor-pressure increase; it is not a new synthetic specimen. The authors instead propose enhanced nonequilibrium steady-state vapor pressure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Nano-Al characterization, footnote 6 and Kelvin discussion

intuition.title: Whiskers versus polycrystalline fibers
intuition.text: SAD establishes single crystallinity for the examined whiskers; study-wide whisker diameters are generally 20–100 nm with aspect ratios 20 to greater than 100. SEM alone cannot establish whether the stubble on partially nitrided Al droplets is single-crystal whiskers. TEM fragments show that some similar material is polycrystalline fibers. These observations remain separate rather than relabeling all fibers as whiskers.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Whisker dimensions, partial-reaction discussion and footnote 14

intuition.title: Scope of practical implications
intuition.text: The paper demonstrates morphological control by varying feed size, chloride addition and ramp rate. It does not measure device, thermal, optical or mechanical performance of the resulting particles. The precursor preparation also has a source-reported explosion warning; the referenced six-page SI with detailed precautions and synthetic procedures remains unreviewed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction, conclusion, footnote 5 and supporting-information notice

intuition.title: Separate grain and interface responses
intuition.text: The authors use annealing to vary the relative amount of nanograins and intercrystalline material, then combine CEMS fractions with iron-projected phonon spectra. They seek to determine whether anomalous low/high-energy vibrations belong to grain interiors or interfaces; the separated spectra depend on a two-component model rather than isolated-grain measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Motivation, CEMS and Equation 1

intuition.title: Thermal history changes more than grain diameter
intuition.text: For samples A–D, the fitted interface atomic fraction drops from 0.51 to 0.11 while mean grain size grows from 10.9 to 14.9 nm. The authors interpret this as an increase mainly in grain number/fraction. The as-quenched material already contains 2.2 nm grains. DSC transitions 783(1) K and 1017(1) K are characterization results, not missing synthesis setpoints.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Table I, preparation and annealing discussion

intuition.title: Model assumption and internal checks
intuition.text: Equation 1 writes g(E)=(1−XIC)gNG(E)+XICgIC(E). Reference grain/interface spectra are derived using A and C, initially assuming only weak variation with grain size. Figures 3–4 compare the as-quenched, B and D component spectra with those references. This assumption and subsequent tests must remain visible when reusing the spectra.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Equation1 and Figures2b,3,4

intuition.title: Thin interfaces can acquire grain-like vibrations
intuition.text: The derived interface spectrum for D, whose mean model thickness is 0.6(5) nm, develops peaks near 23, 27 and 36 meV and loses low-energy states below 20 meV. The authors suggest that an interface about two atomic layers or thinner can acquire neighboring-grain vibrational properties. This is an interpretation of the component model, not an atom-resolved interface image.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure4c and thickness interpretation

intuition.title: Interface fraction, low-energy modes and design implications
intuition.text: The fitted low-energy DOS remains quadratic over 2–12 meV. The normalized coefficient varies approximately linearly with interface fraction; extrapolated endpoints are 1 for bulk Fe and 2.9 for the reference interface spectrum. The authors therefore propose controlling grain fraction to tune thermoelastic behavior. Entropy, displacement, force-constant and specific-heat trends are mentioned without numerical sample results and are not exported as extra measured properties.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure5, low-energy analysis and conclusion

intuition.title: Measurement basis and missing chemical detail
intuition.text: The measured DOS is Fe-projected: B and Zr contributions are excluded by definition (note 23). The source reports 63% enrichment of iron in 57Fe, but no raw-alloy synthesis or detailed melt-spinning settings. Reported grain lattice constants refer to α-Fe, not to a crystalline Fe90Zr7B3 unit cell. No specimen atom coordinates, TEM image or grain-shape distribution is supplied in this main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, Preparation, structural methods and note23

intuition.title: Thickness trend is not globally monotonic
intuition.text: Table I gives 1.0(5) nm for the as-quenched interface and 2.3(5) nm for A; note 19 explains that the derived thickness depends on grain size as well as interface fraction. The subsequent A–D decrease must not be misrepresented as a monotonic decrease from the as-quenched state.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, TableI and note19

intuition.title: Separate grain and interface responses
intuition.text: The authors use annealing to vary the relative amount of nanograins and intercrystalline material, then combine CEMS fractions with iron-projected phonon spectra. They seek to determine whether anomalous low/high-energy vibrations belong to grain interiors or interfaces; the separated spectra depend on a two-component model rather than isolated-grain measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Motivation, CEMS and Equation 1

intuition.title: Thermal history changes more than grain diameter
intuition.text: For samples A–D, the fitted interface atomic fraction drops from 0.51 to 0.11 while mean grain size grows from 10.9 to 14.9 nm. The authors interpret this as an increase mainly in grain number/fraction. The as-quenched material already contains 2.2 nm grains. DSC transitions 783(1) K and 1017(1) K are characterization results, not missing synthesis setpoints.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Table I, preparation and annealing discussion

intuition.title: Model assumption and internal checks
intuition.text: Equation 1 writes g(E)=(1−XIC)gNG(E)+XICgIC(E). Reference grain/interface spectra are derived using A and C, initially assuming only weak variation with grain size. Figures 3–4 compare the as-quenched, B and D component spectra with those references. This assumption and subsequent tests must remain visible when reusing the spectra.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Equation1 and Figures2b,3,4

intuition.title: Thin interfaces can acquire grain-like vibrations
intuition.text: The derived interface spectrum for D, whose mean model thickness is 0.6(5) nm, develops peaks near 23, 27 and 36 meV and loses low-energy states below 20 meV. The authors suggest that an interface about two atomic layers or thinner can acquire neighboring-grain vibrational properties. This is an interpretation of the component model, not an atom-resolved interface image.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure4c and thickness interpretation

intuition.title: Interface fraction, low-energy modes and design implications
intuition.text: The fitted low-energy DOS remains quadratic over 2–12 meV. The normalized coefficient varies approximately linearly with interface fraction; extrapolated endpoints are 1 for bulk Fe and 2.9 for the reference interface spectrum. The authors therefore propose controlling grain fraction to tune thermoelastic behavior. Entropy, displacement, force-constant and specific-heat trends are mentioned without numerical sample results and are not exported as extra measured properties.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure5, low-energy analysis and conclusion

intuition.title: Measurement basis and missing chemical detail
intuition.text: The measured DOS is Fe-projected: B and Zr contributions are excluded by definition (note 23). The source reports 63% enrichment of iron in 57Fe, but no raw-alloy synthesis or detailed melt-spinning settings. Reported grain lattice constants refer to α-Fe, not to a crystalline Fe90Zr7B3 unit cell. No specimen atom coordinates, TEM image or grain-shape distribution is supplied in this main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, Preparation, structural methods and note23

intuition.title: Thickness trend is not globally monotonic
intuition.text: Table I gives 1.0(5) nm for the as-quenched interface and 2.3(5) nm for A; note 19 explains that the derived thickness depends on grain size as well as interface fraction. The subsequent A–D decrease must not be misrepresented as a monotonic decrease from the as-quenched state.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, TableI and note19

intuition.text: Equation 1 writes g(E)=(1−XIC)gNG(E)+XICgIC(E). Reference grain/interface spectra are derived using A and C, initially assuming only weak variation with grain size. Figures 3–4 compare the as-quenched, B and D component spectra with those references. This assumption and subsequent tests must remain visible when reusing the spectra.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Equation1 and Figures2b,3,4

intuition.title: Thin interfaces can acquire grain-like vibrations
intuition.text: The derived interface spectrum for D, whose mean model thickness is 0.6(5) nm, develops peaks near 23, 27 and 36 meV and loses low-energy states below 20 meV. The authors suggest that an interface about two atomic layers or thinner can acquire neighboring-grain vibrational properties. This is an interpretation of the component model, not an atom-resolved interface image.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure4c and thickness interpretation

intuition.title: Interface fraction, low-energy modes and design implications
intuition.text: The fitted low-energy DOS remains quadratic over 2–12 meV. The normalized coefficient varies approximately linearly with interface fraction; extrapolated endpoints are 1 for bulk Fe and 2.9 for the reference interface spectrum. The authors therefore propose controlling grain fraction to tune thermoelastic behavior. Entropy, displacement, force-constant and specific-heat trends are mentioned without numerical sample results and are not exported as extra measured properties.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure5, low-energy analysis and conclusion

intuition.title: Measurement basis and missing chemical detail
intuition.text: The measured DOS is Fe-projected: B and Zr contributions are excluded by definition (note 23). The source reports 63% enrichment of iron in 57Fe, but no raw-alloy synthesis or detailed melt-spinning settings. Reported grain lattice constants refer to α-Fe, not to a crystalline Fe90Zr7B3 unit cell. No specimen atom coordinates, TEM image or grain-shape distribution is supplied in this main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, Preparation, structural methods and note23

intuition.title: Thickness trend is not globally monotonic
intuition.text: Table I gives 1.0(5) nm for the as-quenched interface and 2.3(5) nm for A; note 19 explains that the derived thickness depends on grain size as well as interface fraction. The subsequent A–D decrease must not be misrepresented as a monotonic decrease from the as-quenched state.

intuition.title: Separate grain and interface responses
intuition.text: The authors use annealing to vary the relative amount of nanograins and intercrystalline material, then combine CEMS fractions with iron-projected phonon spectra. They seek to determine whether anomalous low/high-energy vibrations belong to grain interiors or interfaces; the separated spectra depend on a two-component model rather than isolated-grain measurements.

intuition.title: Thermal history changes more than grain diameter
intuition.text: For samples A–D, the fitted interface atomic fraction drops from 0.51 to 0.11 while mean grain size grows from 10.9 to 14.9 nm. The authors interpret this as an increase mainly in grain number/fraction. The as-quenched material already contains 2.2 nm grains. DSC transitions 783(1) K and 1017(1) K are characterization results, not missing synthesis setpoints.

intuition.title: Separate grain and interface responses
intuition.text: The authors use annealing to vary the relative amount of nanograins and intercrystalline material, then combine CEMS fractions with iron-projected phonon spectra. They seek to determine whether anomalous low/high-energy vibrations belong to grain interiors or interfaces; the separated spectra depend on a two-component model rather than isolated-grain measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Motivation, CEMS and Equation 1

intuition.title: Thermal history changes more than grain diameter
intuition.text: For samples A–D, the fitted interface atomic fraction drops from 0.51 to 0.11 while mean grain size grows from 10.9 to 14.9 nm. The authors interpret this as an increase mainly in grain number/fraction. The as-quenched material already contains 2.2 nm grains. DSC transitions 783(1) K and 1017(1) K are characterization results, not missing synthesis setpoints.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Table I, preparation and annealing discussion

intuition.title: Model assumption and internal checks
intuition.text: Equation 1 writes g(E)=(1−XIC)gNG(E)+XICgIC(E). Reference grain/interface spectra are derived using A and C, initially assuming only weak variation with grain size. Figures 3–4 compare the as-quenched, B and D component spectra with those references. This assumption and subsequent tests must remain visible when reusing the spectra.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Equation1 and Figures2b,3,4

intuition.title: Thin interfaces can acquire grain-like vibrations
intuition.text: The derived interface spectrum for D, whose mean model thickness is 0.6(5) nm, develops peaks near 23, 27 and 36 meV and loses low-energy states below 20 meV. The authors suggest that an interface about two atomic layers or thinner can acquire neighboring-grain vibrational properties. This is an interpretation of the component model, not an atom-resolved interface image.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure4c and thickness interpretation

intuition.title: Interface fraction, low-energy modes and design implications
intuition.text: The fitted low-energy DOS remains quadratic over 2–12 meV. The normalized coefficient varies approximately linearly with interface fraction; extrapolated endpoints are 1 for bulk Fe and 2.9 for the reference interface spectrum. The authors therefore propose controlling grain fraction to tune thermoelastic behavior. Entropy, displacement, force-constant and specific-heat trends are mentioned without numerical sample results and are not exported as extra measured properties.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure5, low-energy analysis and conclusion

intuition.title: Measurement basis and missing chemical detail
intuition.text: The measured DOS is Fe-projected: B and Zr contributions are excluded by definition (note 23). The source reports 63% enrichment of iron in 57Fe, but no raw-alloy synthesis or detailed melt-spinning settings. Reported grain lattice constants refer to α-Fe, not to a crystalline Fe90Zr7B3 unit cell. No specimen atom coordinates, TEM image or grain-shape distribution is supplied in this main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, Preparation, structural methods and note23

intuition.title: Thickness trend is not globally monotonic
intuition.text: Table I gives 1.0(5) nm for the as-quenched interface and 2.3(5) nm for A; note 19 explains that the derived thickness depends on grain size as well as interface fraction. The subsequent A–D decrease must not be misrepresented as a monotonic decrease from the as-quenched state.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1,4, TableI and note19

intuition.title: Crystallite and particle sizes describe different measurements
intuition.text: Sample A has a reported Scherrer crystallite size of 5.3 nm and a TEM particle size of about 8 nm; sample B has 3.5 nm and around 5 nm, respectively. The source initially calls these consistent and later notes the TEM values are slightly larger. No exact equivalence, combined average, confidence interval or numerical distribution width is inferred.

intuition.title: Solvent effects and radical pathways are proposed

intuition.text: The authors use a PEG-gel precursor and air calcination to obtain a series of lithium-ferrite crystal sizes. intuition.title: Thermal analysis is evidence about the precursor
intuition.text: The source assigns thermal events to nitrate/PEG decomposition and ferrite formation. This DTA experiment is heated in oxygen at 10 °C/min; its atmosphere and ramp must not be copied into the separately reported air-calcination recipe. The plotted formation event at 303 °C is an analytical assignment, not a universal synthesis setpoint.

intuition.title: Size-dependent magnetism and a source-proposed surface explanation
intuition.text: The authors observe lower saturation magnetization for smaller crystals and suggest a surface effect, citing reference 5. intuition.title: Separate the cluster size from primary crystal size
intuition.text: The authors assemble primary magnetite crystals into larger flowerlike clusters. TEM measures the overall cluster diameter, whereas HRTEM or Scherrer estimates describe the primary crystals. These sizes remain distinct: a 93 nm cluster has a reported 9.65 nm Scherrer grain size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Cluster model, Figures 1–3

intuition.title: Why use poly(acrylic acid)
intuition.text: The authors attribute the PAA choice to coordination of carboxylate groups with iron cations on magnetite. Uncoordinated carboxylate groups extending into water are proposed to provide dispersibility. Surface coverage, chain configuration and a unique polymer molecular graph are not measured.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, PAA discussion

intuition.title: Proposed hydrolysis and growth mechanism
intuition.text: The paper proposes that hot DEG/FeCl3/PAA with NaOH produces water and increases alkalinity, favoring hydrolysis. DEG is proposed to partly reduce Fe(OH)3 to Fe(OH)2, followed by dehydration to Fe3O4. Primary crystals then nucleate and aggregate into clusters; HRTEM alignment is interpreted as oriented attachment with subsequent high-temperature sintering. These are source interpretations, not directly isolated intermediate recipes.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Hydrolysis/growth discussion, Figure 2; cited references 3, 6, 19 and 20

intuition.title: Stock aliquot controls the reported cluster series
intuition.text: Keeping the other stated method conditions fixed, the paper varies NaOH/DEG aliquot volume from 1.60 to 1.85 mL and reports six cluster diameters from 31 to 174 nm. The suggested explanation is a change in water concentration and alkalinity that affects FeCl3 hydrolysis. Neither pH nor water concentration is quantitatively measured in the main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 4, Size-control discussion and Experimental Section

intuition.title: Magnetic response without a large single crystal
intuition.text: The cluster series remains superparamagnetic at room temperature despite its larger overall size. The authors compare strong cluster magnetic response with an 8 nm reference nanodot, and propose that interactions among the primary crystals differ from those of a single crystal. The 93 nm sample has remanence and coercivity at 2 K. No measured critical size for every cluster or temperature-dependent phase change is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3, Magnetic discussion and Figure 4

intuition.title: Mass normalization and fitted moment have different meanings
intuition.text: Saturation magnetization is reported per gram of PAA-covered particles. The paper suggests higher polymer mass fraction or surface disorder as possible reasons for lower small-particle values. Moment per cluster is separately obtained from a Langevin fit and is an author-derived result. The SI fit details and XAS data are not reviewed in this main-only contribution.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4c and adjacent discussion

intuition.title: Application outlook is distinct from demonstrated performance
intuition.text: The authors propose uses in separation, targeted delivery and MRI, as well as future silica coating for ligand coupling. The main demonstrates field-induced chaining, magnetic separation and redispersion; it does not provide a biomedical validation, silica-shell synthesis or ligand-coupling recipe.

intuition.title: Separate the cluster size from primary crystal size
intuition.text: The authors assemble primary magnetite crystals into larger flowerlike clusters. TEM measures the overall cluster diameter, whereas HRTEM or Scherrer estimates describe the primary crystals. These sizes remain distinct: a 93 nm cluster has a reported 9.65 nm Scherrer grain size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Cluster model, Figures 1–3

intuition.title: Why use poly(acrylic acid)
intuition.text: The authors attribute the PAA choice to coordination of carboxylate groups with iron cations on magnetite. Uncoordinated carboxylate groups extending into water are proposed to provide dispersibility. Surface coverage, chain configuration and a unique polymer molecular graph are not measured.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, PAA discussion

intuition.title: Proposed hydrolysis and growth mechanism
intuition.text: The paper proposes that hot DEG/FeCl3/PAA with NaOH produces water and increases alkalinity, favoring hydrolysis. DEG is proposed to partly reduce Fe(OH)3 to Fe(OH)2, followed by dehydration to Fe3O4. Primary crystals then nucleate and aggregate into clusters; HRTEM alignment is interpreted as oriented attachment with subsequent high-temperature sintering. These are source interpretations, not directly isolated intermediate recipes.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Hydrolysis/growth discussion, Figure 2; cited references 3, 6, 19 and 20

intuition.title: Stock aliquot controls the reported cluster series
intuition.text: Keeping the other stated method conditions fixed, the paper varies NaOH/DEG aliquot volume from 1.60 to 1.85 mL and reports six cluster diameters from 31 to 174 nm. The suggested explanation is a change in water concentration and alkalinity that affects FeCl3 hydrolysis. Neither pH nor water concentration is quantitatively measured in the main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 4, Size-control discussion and Experimental Section

intuition.title: Magnetic response without a large single crystal
intuition.text: The cluster series remains superparamagnetic at room temperature despite its larger overall size. The authors compare strong cluster magnetic response with an 8 nm reference nanodot, and propose that interactions among the primary crystals differ from those of a single crystal. The 93 nm sample has remanence and coercivity at 2 K. No measured critical size for every cluster or temperature-dependent phase change is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3, Magnetic discussion and Figure 4

intuition.title: Mass normalization and fitted moment have different meanings
intuition.text: Saturation magnetization is reported per gram of PAA-covered particles. The paper suggests higher polymer mass fraction or surface disorder as possible reasons for lower small-particle values. Moment per cluster is separately obtained from a Langevin fit and is an author-derived result. The SI fit details and XAS data are not reviewed in this main-only contribution.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4c and adjacent discussion

intuition.title: Application outlook is distinct from demonstrated performance
intuition.text: The authors propose uses in separation, targeted delivery and MRI, as well as future silica coating for ligand coupling. The main demonstrates field-induced chaining, magnetic separation and redispersion; it does not provide a biomedical validation, silica-shell synthesis or ligand-coupling recipe.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure 5 and outlook; reference 21

intuition.title: Separate the cluster size from primary crystal size
intuition.text: The authors assemble primary magnetite crystals into larger flowerlike clusters. TEM measures the overall cluster diameter, whereas HRTEM or Scherrer estimates describe the primary crystals. These sizes remain distinct: a 93 nm cluster has a reported 9.65 nm Scherrer grain size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Cluster model, Figures 1–3

intuition.title: Why use poly(acrylic acid)
intuition.text: The authors attribute the PAA choice to coordination of carboxylate groups with iron cations on magnetite. Uncoordinated carboxylate groups extending into water are proposed to provide dispersibility. Surface coverage, chain configuration and a unique polymer molecular graph are not measured.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, PAA discussion

intuition.title: Proposed hydrolysis and growth mechanism
intuition.text: The paper proposes that hot DEG/FeCl3/PAA with NaOH produces water and increases alkalinity, favoring hydrolysis. DEG is proposed to partly reduce Fe(OH)3 to Fe(OH)2, followed by dehydration to Fe3O4. Primary crystals then nucleate and aggregate into clusters; HRTEM alignment is interpreted as oriented attachment with subsequent high-temperature sintering. These are source interpretations, not directly isolated intermediate recipes.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Hydrolysis/growth discussion, Figure 2; cited references 3, 6, 19 and 20

intuition.title: Stock aliquot controls the reported cluster series
intuition.text: Keeping the other stated method conditions fixed, the paper varies NaOH/DEG aliquot volume from 1.60 to 1.85 mL and reports six cluster diameters from 31 to 174 nm. The suggested explanation is a change in water concentration and alkalinity that affects FeCl3 hydrolysis. Neither pH nor water concentration is quantitatively measured in the main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 4, Size-control discussion and Experimental Section

intuition.title: Magnetic response without a large single crystal
intuition.text: The cluster series remains superparamagnetic at room temperature despite its larger overall size. The authors compare strong cluster magnetic response with an 8 nm reference nanodot, and propose that interactions among the primary crystals differ from those of a single crystal. The 93 nm sample has remanence and coercivity at 2 K. No measured critical size for every cluster or temperature-dependent phase change is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3, Magnetic discussion and Figure 4

intuition.title: Mass normalization and fitted moment have different meanings
intuition.text: Saturation magnetization is reported per gram of PAA-covered particles. The paper suggests higher polymer mass fraction or surface disorder as possible reasons for lower small-particle values. Moment per cluster is separately obtained from a Langevin fit and is an author-derived result. The SI fit details and XAS data are not reviewed in this main-only contribution.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4c and adjacent discussion

intuition.title: Application outlook is distinct from demonstrated performance
intuition.text: The authors propose uses in separation, targeted delivery and MRI, as well as future silica coating for ligand coupling. The main demonstrates field-induced chaining, magnetic separation and redispersion; it does not provide a biomedical validation, silica-shell synthesis or ligand-coupling recipe.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure 5 and outlook; reference 21

intuition.title: Separate the cluster size from primary crystal size
intuition.text: The authors assemble primary magnetite crystals into larger flowerlike clusters. TEM measures the overall cluster diameter, whereas HRTEM or Scherrer estimates describe the primary crystals. These sizes remain distinct: a 93 nm cluster has a reported 9.65 nm Scherrer grain size.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–3, Cluster model, Figures 1–3

intuition.title: Why use poly(acrylic acid)
intuition.text: The authors attribute the PAA choice to coordination of carboxylate groups with iron cations on magnetite. Uncoordinated carboxylate groups extending into water are proposed to provide dispersibility. Surface coverage, chain configuration and a unique polymer molecular graph are not measured.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, PAA discussion

intuition.title: Proposed hydrolysis and growth mechanism
intuition.text: The paper proposes that hot DEG/FeCl3/PAA with NaOH produces water and increases alkalinity, favoring hydrolysis. DEG is proposed to partly reduce Fe(OH)3 to Fe(OH)2, followed by dehydration to Fe3O4. Primary crystals then nucleate and aggregate into clusters; HRTEM alignment is interpreted as oriented attachment with subsequent high-temperature sintering. These are source interpretations, not directly isolated intermediate recipes.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Hydrolysis/growth discussion, Figure 2; cited references 3, 6, 19 and 20

intuition.title: Stock aliquot controls the reported cluster series
intuition.text: Keeping the other stated method conditions fixed, the paper varies NaOH/DEG aliquot volume from 1.60 to 1.85 mL and reports six cluster diameters from 31 to 174 nm. The suggested explanation is a change in water concentration and alkalinity that affects FeCl3 hydrolysis. Neither pH nor water concentration is quantitatively measured in the main.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 4, Size-control discussion and Experimental Section

intuition.title: Magnetic response without a large single crystal
intuition.text: The cluster series remains superparamagnetic at room temperature despite its larger overall size. The authors compare strong cluster magnetic response with an 8 nm reference nanodot, and propose that interactions among the primary crystals differ from those of a single crystal. The 93 nm sample has remanence and coercivity at 2 K. No measured critical size for every cluster or temperature-dependent phase change is inferred.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3, Magnetic discussion and Figure 4

intuition.title: Mass normalization and fitted moment have different meanings
intuition.text: Saturation magnetization is reported per gram of PAA-covered particles. The paper suggests higher polymer mass fraction or surface disorder as possible reasons for lower small-particle values. Moment per cluster is separately obtained from a Langevin fit and is an author-derived result. The SI fit details and XAS data are not reviewed in this main-only contribution.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4c and adjacent discussion

intuition.title: Application outlook is distinct from demonstrated performance
intuition.text: The authors propose uses in separation, targeted delivery and MRI, as well as future silica coating for ligand coupling. The main demonstrates field-induced chaining, magnetic separation and redispersion; it does not provide a biomedical validation, silica-shell synthesis or ligand-coupling recipe.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Figure 5 and outlook; reference 21

intuition.title: Why use colloidal PbSe quantum dots
intuition.text: The authors motivate PbSe by its strong confinement and infrared transitions. They cite electron, hole and exciton Bohr radii of 23, 23 and 46 nm and describe a 3–8 nm colloidal size range. These are background/model scales, not particle-coordinate measurements. The source’s stated R/aB range is retained without recalculation or redefinition.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, Introduction and reported confinement range

intuition.title: Temperature controls a series, not a supplied exact sample schedule
intuition.text: The paper varies injection and growth temperature within 80–150 °C and holds growth for 5–10 min. Higher temperatures produce larger dots, but it does not provide an exact temperature/time for each displayed size. The resulting record preserves that relationship without assigning endpoint temperatures to particular specimens.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Synthesis and size-control paragraphs

intuition.title: Single injection and purification
intuition.text: Lead acetate and oleic acid are heated in phenyl ether, cooled, mixed with the reported TOPSe stock, then injected into hot phenyl ether. The paper gives syringe capacity but no measured precursor volume. Repeated precipitation and centrifugation remove excess reagents; size-selective precipitation is stated to be unnecessary under favorable conditions, not mandatory as a separate unreported step.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Synthesis and analytical sample preparation

intuition.title: Structural evidence includes residual precursor
intuition.text: XRD is assigned to rock-salt PbSe and explicitly shows trace lead-oleate precursor peaks. STEM shows a close-packed ensemble and an approximately 7 nm lattice-resolved particle. The authors interpret its Pb-column image as a single crystal without internal defects, but no batch-wide defect fraction, shape distribution or atomic coordinate refinement is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 1–2 and structure discussion

intuition.title: Optical transitions are not all uniquely assigned
intuition.text: The authors compare the approximately 8 nm absorption spectrum with Kang’s model. First and third transitions agree, while the second feature is not accounted for by the allowed-transition calculation. Parity-forbidden transitions and band anisotropy are discussed as alternatives; the article favors the former but states that no decisive assignment is made. Model arrows and bars are not additional measured materials.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and transition interpretation; references 15 and 22

intuition.title: High quantum yield does not prove a measured surface structure
intuition.text: The main reports room-temperature quantum yields of 12–81% without an inorganic semiconductor shell. Variation in surface reconstruction at reaction termination is suggested as an explanation, with comparison to earlier CdSe work. Actual surface reconstruction, ligand coverage and a per-size QY table are not measured.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 5 and quantum-yield discussion; reference 27

intuition.title: Long-lived emission and the later theoretical note
intuition.text: The 3 nm decay shown in Figure 6 has a 250 ns fitted time constant. The authors estimate an unscreened lowest-exciton transition-dipole radiative lifetime on the order of nanoseconds. They estimate that dielectric screening could increase it by as much as two orders of magnitude if bulk PbSe dielectric constants are assumed, while explicitly questioning whether bulk parameters apply to these nanocrystals. These are theoretical estimates, not additional measured lifetimes. Reference 28 adds a note that later calculations account for approximately 0.1 µs decay times; that cited full paper is not reviewed in this contribution, so the note remains source-attributed rather than independently confirmed.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Figure 6, decay discussion and reference 28

intuition.title: Stokes shifts and application outlook remain qualified
intuition.text: Ensemble Stokes shifts of 40–90 meV are reported, but excitation well above the lowest exciton prevents direct identification with an intrinsic single-particle spectrum. Vibronic/non-Franck–Condon effects are proposed. Optoelectronics and fluorescence microscopy are motivations; no device performance or biological test is reported here.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1, 3–4, Abstract, Stokes-shift discussion and outlook; reference 23

intuition.title: Seed enlargement has a finite useful range
intuition.text: One additional precursor injection increases a reported 4.0 nm seed population to 6.2 nm. More than two added injections gives about 10 nm irregular, polydisperse polycrystalline particles. The main SI declaration names three additions, but the SI itself is unreviewed. The 7.2 nm diffraction inset label is not assigned to an invented two-addition recipe.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–4, 6, Additional injections and SI declaration

intuition.title: Alloy assignment and the remaining alternative
intuition.text: ICP-AES and EDX report an approximately 1:3 Co/Pt ratio across the preparations. XRD and HRTEM support chemically disordered fcc CoPt3. The authors explicitly note that diffraction alone cannot completely exclude phase segregation or a core–shell model, then argue against those alternatives using TEM contrast and composition behavior. No measured atomic coordinates, ordered L12 cell or core–shell interface is asserted.

intuition.title: Bulky carboxylate and dynamic amine roles
intuition.text: The authors propose that bulky adamantanecarboxylate provides steric stabilization while more dynamic HDA binding supports a soluble colloid. ACA-only particles are crystalline but polydisperse and poorly soluble; HDA or dodecylamine restores a clear colloid, whereas extra ACA does not. This is a source interpretation, not a measured ligand coverage or unique conformation.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Ligand comparisons and proposed stabilization

intuition.title: Injection temperature versus heating time
intuition.text: Higher injection temperature gives smaller, more uniform particles in the reported HDA/DPE and TDPA/DPE families. The authors discuss nucleation and growth separation. Heating for 1 min, 40 min or 3 h changes nanowire abundance more strongly than the spherical-particle sizes; missing table continuation cells remain explicitly inherited.

intuition.title: Bulky carboxylate and dynamic amine roles
intuition.text: The authors propose that bulky adamantanecarboxylate provides steric stabilization while more dynamic HDA binding supports a soluble colloid. ACA-only particles are crystalline but polydisperse and poorly soluble; HDA or dodecylamine restores a clear colloid, whereas extra ACA does not. This is a source interpretation, not a measured ligand coverage or unique conformation.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Ligand comparisons and proposed stabilization

intuition.title: Alloy assignment and the remaining alternative
intuition.text: ICP-AES and EDX report an approximately 1:3 Co/Pt ratio across the preparations. XRD and HRTEM support chemically disordered fcc CoPt3. The authors explicitly note that diffraction alone cannot completely exclude phase segregation or a core–shell model, then argue against those alternatives using TEM contrast and composition behavior. No measured atomic coordinates, ordered L12 cell or core–shell interface is asserted.

intuition.title: Bulky carboxylate and dynamic amine roles
intuition.text: The authors propose that bulky adamantanecarboxylate provides steric stabilization while more dynamic HDA binding supports a soluble colloid. ACA-only particles are crystalline but polydisperse and poorly soluble; HDA or dodecylamine restores a clear colloid, whereas extra ACA does not. This is a source interpretation, not a measured ligand coverage or unique conformation.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Ligand comparisons and proposed stabilization

intuition.title: Injection temperature versus heating time
intuition.text: Higher injection temperature gives smaller, more uniform particles in the reported HDA/DPE and TDPA/DPE families. The authors discuss nucleation and growth separation. Heating for 1 min, 40 min or 3 h changes nanowire abundance more strongly than the spherical-particle sizes; missing table continuation cells remain explicitly inherited.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Table 1 and temperature/time discussion

intuition.title: Alloy assignment and the remaining alternative
intuition.text: ICP-AES and EDX report an approximately 1:3 Co/Pt ratio across the preparations. XRD and HRTEM support chemically disordered fcc CoPt3. The authors explicitly note that diffraction alone cannot completely exclude phase segregation or a core–shell model, then argue against those alternatives using TEM contrast and composition behavior. No measured atomic coordinates, ordered L12 cell or core–shell interface is asserted.

intuition.title: Bulky carboxylate and dynamic amine roles
intuition.text: The authors propose that bulky adamantanecarboxylate provides steric stabilization while more dynamic HDA binding supports a soluble colloid. ACA-only particles are crystalline but polydisperse and poorly soluble; HDA or dodecylamine restores a clear colloid, whereas extra ACA does not. This is a source interpretation, not a measured ligand coverage or unique conformation.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Ligand comparisons and proposed stabilization

intuition.title: Injection temperature versus heating time
intuition.text: Higher injection temperature gives smaller, more uniform particles in the reported HDA/DPE and TDPA/DPE families. The authors discuss nucleation and growth separation. Heating for 1 min, 40 min or 3 h changes nanowire abundance more strongly than the spherical-particle sizes; missing table continuation cells remain explicitly inherited.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Table 1 and temperature/time discussion

intuition.title: Alloy assignment and the remaining alternative
intuition.text: ICP-AES and EDX report an approximately 1:3 Co/Pt ratio across the preparations. XRD and HRTEM support chemically disordered fcc CoPt3. The authors explicitly note that diffraction alone cannot completely exclude phase segregation or a core–shell model, then argue against those alternatives using TEM contrast and composition behavior. No measured atomic coordinates, ordered L12 cell or core–shell interface is asserted.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Structural characterization; Figure 2

intuition.title: Bulky carboxylate and dynamic amine roles
intuition.text: The authors propose that bulky adamantanecarboxylate provides steric stabilization while more dynamic HDA binding supports a soluble colloid. ACA-only particles are crystalline but polydisperse and poorly soluble; HDA or dodecylamine restores a clear colloid, whereas extra ACA does not. This is a source interpretation, not a measured ligand coverage or unique conformation.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Ligand comparisons and proposed stabilization

intuition.title: Injection temperature versus heating time
intuition.text: Higher injection temperature gives smaller, more uniform particles in the reported HDA/DPE and TDPA/DPE families. The authors discuss nucleation and growth separation. Heating for 1 min, 40 min or 3 h changes nanowire abundance more strongly than the spherical-particle sizes; missing table continuation cells remain explicitly inherited.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Table 1 and temperature/time discussion

intuition.title: Alloy assignment and the remaining alternative
intuition.text: ICP-AES and EDX report an approximately 1:3 Co/Pt ratio across the preparations. XRD and HRTEM support chemically disordered fcc CoPt3. The authors explicitly note that diffraction alone cannot completely exclude phase segregation or a core–shell model, then argue against those alternatives using TEM contrast and composition behavior. No measured atomic coordinates, ordered L12 cell or core–shell interface is asserted.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Structural characterization; Figure 2

intuition.title: Fuel loading and powder growth
intuition.text: The authors attribute smaller particles and a narrower distribution at the higher sucrose loading to greater gas evolution that hinders coalescence and growth. This is an interpretation of the 1A/2A comparison, not a quantified gas flow or combustion temperature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, TEM size-distribution discussion

intuition.title: Annealing purity has a documented exception
intuition.text: The detailed XRD analysis reports residual Mn2O3 for 0.5A, which is excluded from further measurements. Only 1A and 2A are described as single-spinel patterns. Broad abstract/conclusion statements about pure annealed products do not erase this exception.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, 4, Abstract, Figure 1 discussion and conclusion

intuition.title: Lithium-rich composition from different observations
intuition.text: TG/reference correlation gives x=0.05 in Li1+xMn2−xO4, lattice-parameter correlation gives x=0.06, and electrochemical capacity gives an estimated Li1.04Mn1.96O4. These are distinct author-derived composition estimates, not independently refined exact site coordinates.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Thermal, chemical and electrochemical composition analyses

intuition.title: Transport mechanisms depend on temperature
intuition.text: The authors fit the 2A-derived pellet above 180 K using nearest-neighbor small-polaron hopping, and below 180 K using variable-range hopping. Model parameters are not new preparation variants; a separately prepared pellet is not assigned the powder TEM diameter.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and equations 2–3

intuition.title: Rate capability and cycling interpretation
intuition.text: Higher current is interpreted as restricting lithium exchange to the outer particle region. The authors relate the small-particle sample’s higher high-rate capacity to its size and its slow capacity fade to lithium excess. The solid-state comparator lacks a complete preparation in the supplied article.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Figures 6–7 and rate/cycling discussion

intuition.text: The authors attribute smaller particles and a narrower distribution at the higher sucrose loading to greater gas evolution that hinders coalescence and growth. This is an interpretation of the 1A/2A comparison, not a quantified gas flow or combustion temperature.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, TEM size-distribution discussion

intuition.title: Annealing purity has a documented exception
intuition.text: The detailed XRD analysis reports residual Mn2O3 for 0.5A, which is excluded from further measurements. Only 1A and 2A are described as single-spinel patterns. Broad abstract/conclusion statements about pure annealed products do not erase this exception.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, 4, Abstract, Figure 1 discussion and conclusion

intuition.title: Lithium-rich composition from different observations
intuition.text: TG/reference correlation gives x=0.05 in Li1+xMn2−xO4, lattice-parameter correlation gives x=0.06, and electrochemical capacity gives an estimated Li1.04Mn1.96O4. These are distinct author-derived composition estimates, not independently refined exact site coordinates.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–4, Thermal, chemical and electrochemical composition analyses

intuition.title: Transport mechanisms depend on temperature
intuition.text: The authors fit the 2A-derived pellet above 180 K using nearest-neighbor small-polaron hopping, and below 180 K using variable-range hopping. Model parameters are not new preparation variants; a separately prepared pellet is not assigned the powder TEM diameter.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 4 and equations 2–3

intuition.title: Rate capability and cycling interpretation
intuition.text: Higher current is interpreted as restricting lithium exchange to the outer particle region. The authors relate the small-particle sample’s higher high-rate capacity to its size and its slow capacity fade to lithium excess. The solid-state comparator lacks a complete preparation in the supplied article.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4, Figures 6–7 and rate/cycling discussion

intuition.title: Two preparation routes, two material outcomes
intuition.text: The PAA-coated NC sample is precipitated from acetate stocks and sulfide, then dried with acrylic acid. SMP is made by treating existing ZnS particles with manganese acetate and ammonia, followed by nitrogen firing. The two EPR signals are coordination environments within a sample, not additional syntheses.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Preparation, Table 2 and EPR assignment

intuition.title: Quantum confinement and the imperfect-coating possibility
intuition.text: The authors relate the higher-energy NC excitation band to quantum confinement. Its reported 3.78 eV peak differs from a 4.2 eV effective-mass prediction based on measured size; they discuss coagulation and imperfect PAA coating as possible explanations. The 4.2 eV prediction and cited approximately 2.5 nm exciton Bohr radius are model/reference context, not new measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and size discussion

intuition.title: Symmetry and dopant-site interpretation
intuition.text: Signal I is assigned to substitutional Mn2+ coordinated by four sulfide ions in cubic ZnS. Larger zero-field splitting and lattice distortion in NC are interpreted as lower crystal-field symmetry. Signal II, detected only for NC at Q-band, is assigned to near-surface Mn2+; its larger hyperfine splitting is linked to more ionic coordination.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–5, Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–6

intuition.title: Polymer coordination and oxidation
intuition.text: The source compares sulfate-related IR bands in uncoated ZnS:Mn with the PAA-coated NC spectrum and proposes carboxyl oxygen coordination near Mn sites. Cited prior XPS evidence is not newly measured in this main. This is a source-attributed coordination interpretation, not an atom-resolved shell structure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–5, Figure 6 and oxygen-coordination discussion

intuition.title: Temperature-independent EPR linewidth and energy transfer
intuition.text: NC signals I and II show little linewidth change while SMP signal I narrows on cooling. With the assumption of a temperature-independent spin–spin term, the authors infer stronger spin–lattice interactions and more effective ZnS–Mn and PAA–Mn energy transfer. No numerical T1 lifetime or fitted temperature exponent is reported.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 5–6, Figure 7 and relaxation discussion

intuition.title: Relative luminescence is not absolute quantum yield
intuition.text: The source reports sevenfold greater NC luminescence under the same stated 350 nm excitation despite lower measured Mn content. It favors greater luminescence efficiency over reduced scattering because these small particles coagulate and acrylic acid accelerates coagulation. No absolute quantum yield or controlled scattering correction is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 1 discussion

intuition.title: Two preparation routes, two material outcomes
intuition.text: The PAA-coated NC sample is precipitated from acetate stocks and sulfide, then dried with acrylic acid. SMP is made by treating existing ZnS particles with manganese acetate and ammonia, followed by nitrogen firing. The two EPR signals are coordination environments within a sample, not additional syntheses.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Preparation, Table 2 and EPR assignment

intuition.title: Quantum confinement and the imperfect-coating possibility
intuition.text: The authors relate the higher-energy NC excitation band to quantum confinement. Its reported 3.78 eV peak differs from a 4.2 eV effective-mass prediction based on measured size; they discuss coagulation and imperfect PAA coating as possible explanations. The 4.2 eV prediction and cited approximately 2.5 nm exciton Bohr radius are model/reference context, not new measurements.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3, Figure 2 and size discussion

intuition.title: Symmetry and dopant-site interpretation
intuition.text: Signal I is assigned to substitutional Mn2+ coordinated by four sulfide ions in cubic ZnS. Larger zero-field splitting and lattice distortion in NC are interpreted as lower crystal-field symmetry. Signal II, detected only for NC at Q-band, is assigned to near-surface Mn2+; its larger hyperfine splitting is linked to more ionic coordination.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 3–5, Tables 1–2 and Figures 3–6

intuition.title: Polymer coordination and oxidation
intuition.text: The source compares sulfate-related IR bands in uncoated ZnS:Mn with the PAA-coated NC spectrum and proposes carboxyl oxygen coordination near Mn sites. Cited prior XPS evidence is not newly measured in this main. This is a source-attributed coordination interpretation, not an atom-resolved shell structure.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 4–5, Figure 6 and oxygen-coordination discussion

intuition.title: Temperature-independent EPR linewidth and energy transfer
intuition.text: NC signals I and II show little linewidth change while SMP signal I narrows on cooling. With the assumption of a temperature-independent spin–spin term, the authors infer stronger spin–lattice interactions and more effective ZnS–Mn and PAA–Mn energy transfer. No numerical T1 lifetime or fitted temperature exponent is reported.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 5–6, Figure 7 and relaxation discussion

intuition.title: Relative luminescence is not absolute quantum yield
intuition.text: The source reports sevenfold greater NC luminescence under the same stated 350 nm excitation despite lower measured Mn content. It favors greater luminescence efficiency over reduced scattering because these small particles coagulate and acrylic acid accelerates coagulation. No absolute quantum yield or controlled scattering correction is supplied.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, Figure 1 discussion

intuition.title: Molecular mixing before oxide formation
intuition.text: The authors use a heterometallic alkoxide with Gd/Fe = 1:1 and existing Gd–O–Fe connections. They argue that atomic-scale cation mixing avoids the intermediate phases possible when separate metal salts are mixed. This is source-attributed synthesis reasoning, not an independently verified reaction mechanism.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 1–2, 4, Introduction, molecular precursor and conclusion

intuition.title: Hydrolysis and thermal conversion
intuition.text: Water activation creates a sol and gel. The authors attribute the thermal-loss stages to solvent loss, removal of alkoxy groups, then dehydroxylation/condensation. A DTA exotherm around 680 °C accompanies oxide crystallization; it is an analytical signal, not an additional synthesis dwell.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2, 5, Thermal discussion and Nanopowder Synthesis

intuition.title: Temperature-dependent ordering and dimensions
intuition.text: The 600 °C powder is amorphous, 700 °C shows initial crystallization and 800 °C shows a developed orthoferrite pattern. The 45, 55 and 70 nm values are XRD crystallite estimates at 800, 1000 and 1200 °C. The approximately 60 nm faceted crystallites in TEM belong specifically to the 1000 °C specimen.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, Figures 2–3 and structural discussion

intuition.title: Phase purity has a defined evidence scope
intuition.text: The diffraction discussion reports no garnet or other crystalline intermediate, and EDX reports no cation segregation at examined spots. These observations do not establish every possible impurity below detection or provide measured atomic coordinates. The molecular precursor cell in Table 1 must not be used as the oxide cell.
intuition.source_locator: Main PDF p. 2–3, 5, XRD/EDX discussion and Table 1

intuition.title: Mixed magnetic contributions
intuition.text: The authors interpret the near-linear response as a dominant Gd paramagnetic contribution plus weak ferromagnetism from canting in the Fe sublattice. Their series-level coercivity and model-derived canting values are retained as context, not assigned as separate precise measurements to both calcination specimens. They report no superparamagnetic response in the examined size range.
